blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Tonight, two kinds of light take the stage: flying robots that paint pictures in the sky, and one tiny insect with its own lamp.
First, a world-record drone show.
Then, the secret of the firefly's cold light.
Ready?
Let's go!
Raise your eyes to the night sky over Dujiangyan in Sichuan, China.
At the approach of night, 33,615 drones rise together into the dark and set three Guinness World Records at once, the largest number of drones ever flown in one show!
Each drone is small, about the size of a sparrow, and carries one bright LED light.
One computer can conduct the whole show, like a conductor leading an orchestra, and every drone holds its own altitude while every aspect is planned in advance.
Watch what they paint: a giant panda munching bamboo, floating islands, and the 28 constellations of the East, star pictures from old Chinese stories.
The lights pulse on and off, and the drones even write a sentence across the sky!
Together, they form a floating screen, the largest mid-air LED screen ever made.
The drones act as one giant paintbrush, quietly: no smoke to make you cough, no loud bangs, just light dancing in the dark.
Now let's meet nature's own little lamp: the firefly.
A firefly is not a fly at all.
It is a beetle, and it carries its light under its belly, in a special tissue, a thin layer of tiny cells.
Here is the secret: inside those cells, two chemicals meet.
One is called luciferin, and the other is an enzyme called luciferase.
Add oxygen from the air, and the mixture gives off light.
Scientists call this bioluminescence, living light.
And here is the magic part: almost all the energy turns into light, and almost none turns into heat.
A normal light bulb wastes most of its energy as heat, but a firefly's light is cold light.
You can hold a firefly in your hand, and its glow will not burn you at all!
Why do they glow?
Mostly to talk.
Each kind of firefly flashes its own code, a pattern of pulses, like a secret language.
Males flash, females answer.
Some mother fireflies, pregnant with tiny eggs, keep flashing to warn hungry birds: do not eat me, I taste terrible!
Each egg she lays is tinier than a grain of rice.
You might think the light sits on its forehead.
No!
It sits under its belly.
Today's idiom is "burn the midnight oil." It means to work or study late into the night.
Long ago, people read by oil lamps, so working after midnight really did burn oil!
For example: The engineers burned the midnight oil for weeks to program 33,615 drones for the record show.
Fireflies never need to burn the midnight oil: they carry their own lights!
Try it this week: tell your family about a time you burned the midnight oil.
Now it is your turn!
Two questions for you.
One: which light would you rather have in your bedroom, a drone show or a firefly lamp?
Two: can you invent your own flash code, maybe two quick flashes for "hello" and three for "good night"?
Talk about it with your family!
Oh, and one more thing: if nature gave a diploma, the firefly would graduate first in its class in chemistry!
That is all for today, young explorers.
We appreciate you listening and learning with us.
Keep your eyes open, keep asking questions, and we will meet again tomorrow morning.
Goodbye, and have a wonderful day!
